alerts.headline: Flood Advisory issued September 26 at 6:23PM HST until September 26 at 9:45PM HST by NWS Honolulu HI
alerts.description:
* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues.

* WHERE...The island of Hawaii in Hawaii County...

* WHEN...Until 945 PM HST.

* IMPACTS...Minor flooding on roads, poor drainage areas, and in
streams. Water over roadways.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 618 PM HST, emergency management reported that portions of
Highway 11 remain closed in both directions due to flooding.
Locations include between Pinao Street and Kaalualu Road in
Waiohinu, as well as between Naalehu and Ninole. Kaalaiki Road
remains closed near the intersection with Highway 11 in Naalehu.
Areas of moderate rain will continue to move into southeast
portions of the Big Island over the next few hours with rainfall
rates generally 0.5 to 1 inch per hour.
- Some locations that will experience flooding include...
Hawaiian Paradise Park, Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, Wood
Valley, Volcano, Pahala, Glenwood, Punaluu Beach, Kawa Flats,
Mountain View and Hawaiian Acres.
alerts.instruction:
Stay away from streams, drainage ditches and low lying areas prone to
flooding.

A Flood Watch is also in effect for until 6 AM HST.

alerts.headline: Flood Watch issued September 26 at 5:26PM HST until September 27 at 6:00AM HST by NWS Honolulu HI
alerts.description:
Hurricane Nolo is now south-southwest of the Big Island and
beginning to move more quickly off to the west. The possibility of
heavy rain could lead to localized flooding over portions of the Big
Island through tonight.

* WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall is possible.

* WHERE...The Big Island.

* WHEN...Through late tonight.

* IMPACTS...Flood prone roads and other low lying areas may be closed
due to elevated runoff and overflowing streams. Urban areas may
receive more significant flooding and property damage due to rapid
runoff.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- The possibility remains for localized flooding over areas of the
Big Island due to heavy rain from Hurricane Nolo to the
south-southwest of the Big Island. Areas most at risk for
flooding are the windward and southeast portions of the Big
Island where the ground remains saturated after recent rains.
alerts.instruction:
You should monitor later forecasts and be prepared to take action
should Flash Flood Warnings be issued.

alerts.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued September 26 at 5:15PM HST by NWS Honolulu HI
alerts.description:
HLSHFO

This product covers the Hawaiian islands

**ALL TROPICAL WATCHES AND WARNINGS HAVE BEEN CANCELLED**


NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- All watches and warnings have been canceled

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 330 miles south-southeast of Honolulu
- 16.7N 156.5W
- Storm Intensity 90 mph
- Movement West or 265 degrees at 8 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Hurricane Nolo is moving west and will pick up speed as it strengthens
into a major hurricane later tonight or early Sunday. Nolo is forecast
to turn toward the northwest Monday and Tuesday. While the center of
Nolo will stay well south and west of the state, strong gusty winds
will still occur due to the tight pressure gradient between Nolo and
high pressure to the north. On Big Island and in Maui County, a
combination of High Wind Warnings for upper terrain and notoriously
windy areas and Wind Advisories for remaining lower elevations will
replace Tropical Storm Watches and Warnings. A Wind Advisory is also
remains in effect for Oahu and Kauai.

Bands of moderate to heavy showers and thunderstorms may bring an
additional 1 to 2 inches, isolated 4 inches, of rainfall to windward
and southeast regions of Big Island. Periods of moderate to locally
heavy rain may spread into Maui, introducing an additional 1 to
2 inches of rain. Localized heavy rain could produce significant
flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain or in
areas that have already experienced flooding during previous storms.
Terrain-enhanced rainfall from Nolo's outer rain bands may also reach
the islands of Oahu and Kauai.

Swell generated by Nolo will bring dangerously large, rough surf and
severe rip currents, especially for the east and south-facing shores
of Big Island. A High Surf Warning is in effect for the south-facing
shores of Big Island. A High Surf Advisory remains in effect for the
east-facing shores of Big Island as well as the east-facing shores of
Maui, Molokai, Oahu and Kauai.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Little to no additional wind impacts expected.
- Community officials are now assessing the extent of actual wind
impacts accordingly.
- Emergency response teams are attending to casualty situations
as needed.
- Emergency work crews are restoring essential community
infrastructure as necessary.
- If you have an emergency dial 9 1 1.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Additional impacts from locally hazardous flooding are still a concern
on Big Island. There is a Flood Watch in effect through tonight for
Big Island.

* TORNADOES:
Little to no impacts are anticipated at this time across the Hawaiian
islands.

* SURGE:
Little to no impacts are anticipated at this time across the Hawaiian
islands.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Remain safely sheltered until conditions improve. When going outside
be sure to stay away from downed power lines, hazardous debris and
flooded areas.

If your home or shelter was damaged, be alert to the smell of gas
leaks and be cautious around electrical wiring, broken glass, jagged
metal and wood, and protruding nails and screws.

Check to see if everyone in your group is OK. Administer first aid to
those who are injured. If possible, call 9 1 1 for any serious
injuries. Remember, it may be difficult for emergency responders to
arrive quickly.

Check in with your emergency points of contact. Let them know your
location and status. Keep conversations short and to the point. Do
not tie up communications systems.

Check on your neighbors. If necessary, help them connect with their
points of contact.

Do not attempt to return to evacuated areas until local authorities
have inspected roads and bridges and have given the all clear.
Hazards like downed power lines and trees, washed out roads,
continued flooding in low lying areas and non-functioning traffic
lights make travel difficult.

Allow extra time for emergency vehicles to reach you as they navigate
road hazards.

Do not attempt to return to evacuated areas until local authorities
give the all clear. Allow time for officials to inspect bridges and
overpasses and to mark washed-out roads.

When entering areas that have been heavily damaged, bring along a
GPS-enabled device to help with street navigation. Do not drive on
roads that have been marked closed.

Do not go sightseeing within impacted communities. Sightseers
interfere with the emergency work of first responders.

When inspecting damage, use flashlights rather than candles or flamed
lanterns. Be aware of sparks that can ignite natural gas or other
leaking flammables.

Do not go up on your roof until the weather conditions are safe.
Ladders can be slippery in the rain and unexpected wind gusts can
blow you off the roof.

When clearing out fallen trees, be careful with chainsaws and axes.
Always wear protective gear and keep others at a safe distance.
Leaning trees and those which have fallen on roofs or power lines can
be especially dangerous. If you are not in good health or unsure
about what you are doing, have someone with tree cutting experience
do the job. Never cut trees without a partner.

If using a generator, avoid carbon monoxide poisoning by following
instructions provided by the manufacturer. Operate your generator in
a well-ventilated space outside of your living area and away from
open doors and windows.

Problems with sewer backups can further contaminate standing flood
waters. Keep children away from flood waters. Also, listen for boil
water alerts as tap water may have become non-potable.

Be alert for any lingering wind gusts which could take down weakened
trees and/or power lines, collapse damaged structures, or cause
flying debris.

Be alert for potential flooding from rising rivers and streams which
may have yet to crest. Remain informed of the latest river forecasts
and heed any flood watches and warnings.

Be alert for flooded roads which could be compromised or littered
with debris. Avoid travel until water levels subside and roads have
been cleared. Do not drive through places where flood waters cover
the road. Turn around, don't drown!

Have multiple ways to receive Tornado Warnings if issued. Consider
nearby shelter options as you move about. Be ready to shelter quickly.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

As it pertains to this event...this will be the last local statement
issued by the National Weather Service in Honolulu HI regarding the
effects of tropical cyclone hazards upon the area.

outlookText:
689 
ACPN50 PHFO 270527
TWOCP 

Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS Central Pacific Hurricane Center Honolulu HI
Issued by NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
800 PM HST Sat Sep 26 2026

For the central North Pacific...between 140W and 180W:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on Hurricane
Polo, located southwest of Cabo San Lucas, Mexico, on Hurricane
Odalys, located well west of the southern tip of Baja California,
and on Hurricane Nolo, located south-southwest of the Big Island of
Hawaii.

Well East-Southeast of the Hawaiian Islands:
A broad area of low pressure located about 1000 miles to the
east-southeast of the Hawaiian Islands is becoming organized.
Environmental conditions are expected to be conducive for
development of this system, and a tropical depression is likely to
form during the early to middle part of next week. The system should
move generally northeastward, and remain well east-southeast of the
Hawaiian Islands.
* Formation chance through 48 hours...medium...40 percent.
* Formation chance through 7 days...high...70 percent.

&&

High Seas Forecasts issued by the National Weather Service
can be found under AWIPS header NFDHSFEPI, WMO header FZPN02
KWBC, and on the web at ocean.weather.gov/shtml/NFDHSFEPI.php

$$
Forecaster Pierce/Evans/Pasch
NNNN
aiBriefing: Aktualne alerty (powódź, silny wiatr, wysoki przybój) są związane z huraganem Nolo, który już oddala się od wysp — wszystkie te ostrzeżenia wygasają dziś (27 września) lub jutro rano, czyli zakończą się na długo przed Waszym wylotem 2 października. Poziom zagrożenia 2 (Podwyższony) odzwierciedla to, co dzieje się teraz, a nie to, co zastaniecie w trakcie podróży. Dodatkowo CPHC wspomina o możliwym nowym układzie pogodowym daleko na wschód-południowy wschód od Hawajów, z 70% szansą uformowania się w cyklon w ciągu 7 dni — ale ten system ma poruszać się na północny wschód i pozostać z dala od wysp, więc na razie nie jest bezpośrednim zagrożeniem dla Waszej trasy. Warto śledzić prognozy bliżej daty wylotu, ale na dziś nie ma podstaw do zmiany planów.

aiUnnamedSystem.description: Słabo zorganizowany niski układ ciśnienia opisany jako będący około 1000 mil (ok. 1600 km) na wschód-południowy wschód od Wysp Hawajskich, z 70% szansą uformowania się w depresję tropikalną w ciągu 7 dni. Prognoza wskazuje ruch na północny wschód, czyli oddalanie się od Hawajów.
